subject: chemistry

items.correct: A molecular entity that has an unpaired electron
items.misconception: A molecular entity that carries an electric charge
items.why: Both radicals and ions are described as 'reactive species', and students meet ions (Cl⁻, Na⁺) years before radicals. A superscript-like dot beside a symbol looks like a charge sign, and radicals are often introduced in the same lessons as heterolytic fission, which does form ions. A radical is defined by having an unpaired electron, not by charge. Count electrons: a Cl atom has 17 electrons and 17 protons, so Cl• is neutral; Cl⁻ has 18 electrons, all paired, and is an ion but not a radical.
items.specStatementText: A radical is a molecular entity that has an unpaired electron. Radicals are highly reactive.
items.random_wrong: A group of atoms that stays together in reactions

items.q: Which species is a radical, and for what reason? Any charge on a species is shown, but unpaired electrons are not marked.
items.correct: C₂H₅, because it has an odd number (13) of valence electrons
items.misconception: BF₃, because boron has only 6, not 8, outer-shell electrons
items.why: The octet rule is taught as the test of whether a species is 'stable', so students treat every departure from an octet as the same kind of instability. Radicals do have incomplete octets (Cl• has seven outer electrons), so the property is mistaken for the definition. Count the electrons and check whether they are all paired. An odd total means an unpaired electron (a radical). An even total with a missing pair, as in BF₃ (24 valence electrons) or CH₃⁺, is electron-deficient but not a radical.
items.specStatementText: A radical is a molecular entity that has an unpaired electron. Radicals are highly reactive.
items.random_wrong: OH⁻, because it has one more electron than a neutral OH group

items.q: Methane reacts with bromine in ultraviolet (UV) light. Which equation represents the initiation step?
items.why: Earlier courses meet bond breaking mainly in ionic contexts (dissolving salts, acids ionizing, electrolysis), and the prefixes homo-/hetero- are easily swapped. Students therefore picture every bond breaking as a split into ions. 'Homo' = the same: each atom gets the same share, one electron each, giving two radicals. 'Hetero' = different: one atom takes both electrons, giving a cation and an anion. Only heterolytic fission produces ions.
items.specStatementText: Radicals are produced by homolytic fission, e.g. of halogens, in the presence of ultraviolet (UV) light or heat.

items.q: In the homolytic fission of Cl₂, two single-barbed (fish-hook) arrows are drawn, each starting at the Cl–Cl bond and ending at a different chlorine atom. What does each arrow represent?
items.misconception: The movement of an electron pair
items.why: Students learn curly arrows (pairs) in most mechanisms and meet fish-hook arrows only in radical reactions, so they treat the half-head as a drawing style rather than a different meaning. The number of barbs counts the electrons moved: one barb, one electron; two barbs, two electrons. Homolytic fission of Cl₂ needs two fish-hook arrows, one electron to each Cl atom.
items.specStatementText: Radicals are produced by homolytic fission, e.g. of halogens, in the presence of ultraviolet (UV) light or heat.
items.random_wrong: The movement of a chlorine atom

items.q: Methane and chlorine react in UV light or on heating. Bond enthalpies: Cl–Cl 242 kJ mol⁻¹; C–H 414 kJ mol⁻¹. Which bond breaks in the initiation step, and why?
items.correct: Cl–Cl breaks, because less energy is needed to break it than to break C–H
items.misconception: C–H breaks, because breaking the stronger bond releases the greater amount of energy
items.why: Biology teaching of ATP and food 'releasing energy' and everyday talk of 'energy stored in bonds' suggest that energy comes out when bonds break. This is one of the most widely documented misconceptions in chemistry-education research. Breaking a bond needs energy equal to its bond enthalpy; forming a bond releases it. That is why UV light or heat is needed for initiation, and why the weaker Cl–Cl bond, not the stronger C–H bond, is the one that breaks.
items.specStatementText: Radicals are produced by homolytic fission, e.g. of halogens, in the presence of ultraviolet (UV) light or heat.
items.random_wrong: Cl–Cl breaks, because the bond splits readily into Cl⁺ and Cl⁻ ions

items.q: Ethane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Which equation represents a propagation step of this reaction?
items.why: The word 'substitution' and the overall equation suggest a simple swap of Cl for H. Writing a propagation step that produces H• is a common error in examination answers. Follow the bonds broken and formed: H–Cl (431 kJ mol⁻¹) forms when Cl• takes H from CH₄, and C–Cl forms when •CH₃ takes Cl from Cl₂. The chain carrier regenerated is Cl•, not H•.
items.specStatementText: Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes, producing a mixture of products.

items.q: A student claims: 'Chlorine radicals are used up in the propagation steps, so every molecule of CH₃Cl formed from methane and chlorine needs a new Cl• from the initiation step.' Which evaluation of this claim is correct?
items.correct: Incorrect: the Cl• used in the first step is re-formed in the second, so it can react again
items.misconception: Correct: each propagation step uses up a radical, so each CH₃Cl needs a new initiation
items.why: In most reactions students meet, a reactant that takes part is consumed. The chain idea, in which a reactive species is regenerated, is unfamiliar, and students do not check the radical count on each side of a propagation equation. Count radicals on each side of each propagation step: one on the left, one on the right. The regenerated Cl• starts another cycle, so one initiation event can lead to thousands of product molecules. Radicals are removed only in termination.
items.specStatementText: Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes, producing a mixture of products.
items.random_wrong: Incorrect: the H• formed in the first step reacts with Cl₂ to re-form Cl• for the chain

items.q: The products of the reaction of methane with chlorine in UV light include CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. How are most of these more highly substituted products formed?
items.correct: Cl• removes an H atom from a chloromethane; the radical then reacts with Cl₂
items.misconception: Chlorinated methyl radicals combine with Cl• in termination, the main source of products
items.why: Students expect the product to appear in the 'final' step, and •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl looks like the obvious way to put a methyl group and a chlorine atom together. Radicals are far outnumbered by Cl₂ and CH₄ molecules, so a radical almost always collides with a molecule (propagation) rather than another radical (termination). The main route to CH₃Cl is •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•.
items.specStatementText: Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes, producing a mixture of products.
items.random_wrong: Cl• replaces an H atom in a chloromethane directly, releasing a free H• radical

items.q: A small amount of ethane, C₂H₆, is found in the product mixture when methane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Which statement explains why ethane is present?
items.correct: Two methyl radicals combine in a termination step: •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆
items.misconception: It is not a reaction product; only CH₃Cl and HCl form, so it is an impurity
items.why: Students read a balanced equation as a complete description of what forms, because most reactions they have met give one product as written. An equation shows one reaction, not everything that happens. Cl• attacks any C–H bond it meets, including those in CH₃Cl, and radicals combine in several ways, so radical substitution always gives a mixture.
items.specStatementText: Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes, producing a mixture of products.
items.random_wrong: A methyl radical replaces H in methane: •CH₃ + CH₄ → C₂H₆ + H•

items.q: Alkanes react with very few reagents. Which statement explains the low reactivity of alkanes?
items.correct: Their C–C and C–H bonds are strong and are essentially non-polar.
items.misconception: They are saturated, and saturated compounds are unreactive.
items.why: Alkanes are introduced alongside alkenes, where 'unsaturated' is linked to reactivity (addition), so students conclude that 'saturated' means 'unreactive'. Saturated means only single bonds between carbon atoms. It says nothing about bond strength or polarity; CH₃CH₂Br and CH₃CH₂OH are saturated but react readily because they contain polar bonds.
items.specStatementText: Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes, producing a mixture of products.
items.random_wrong: Each atom has a full outer shell, so the molecule is unreactive.

items.q: Bromine reacts with methane in ultraviolet (UV) light. The diagram shows two drawings of the Br–Br bond in Br₂ breaking. Which statement about the drawings is correct?
items.correct: Drawing P shows the initiation step, forming two Br• radicals
items.misconception: In Drawing P, each arrow shows one bromine atom moving to a new position
items.why: In everyday diagrams and in reaction equations, arrows show things moving or changing into something else, so students read mechanism arrows as atoms 'moving across'. Chemistry-education research on mechanisms widely reports students using arrows to show atom movement rather than electron movement. Mechanism arrows are electron bookkeeping. Each arrow starts at electrons (a bond or lone pair) and ends where they go; atoms move as a consequence, but the arrow itself shows electrons.
items.specStatementText: Radicals are produced by homolytic fission, e.g. of halogens, in the presence of ultraviolet (UV) light or heat.
items.random_wrong: Br₂ splits into Br⁺ and Br⁻ in the initiation step, as Drawing Q shows

items.q: The diagram shows the electron movements in a propagation step of the reaction of methane with chlorine. Which products does the step shown form?
items.why: Overall equations are learned long before mechanisms, and students assume the equation describes a single collision between the reactants shown. An overall equation is the sum of the steps of the mechanism. For radical substitution, add the two propagation steps: the radical cancels, leaving the overall equation.
items.specStatementText: Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes, producing a mixture of products.

items.q: Does the word 'radical' mean a group of atoms that stays together through a reaction?
items.correct: No. In current chemistry (IUPAC) a radical is a molecular entity with an unpaired electron. A single atom such as Cl• is a radical, and a group such as SO₄²⁻ is not.
items.misconception: A radical is a group of atoms that stays together as a unit in reactions, such as sulfate or ammonium.
items.why: In older chemistry, and in some older school textbooks, "radical" named a group of atoms that passes unchanged through reactions, such as the "sulfate radical" or the "ammonium radical". Students who met this meaning earlier carry it into the IB course. Use the IB (and IUPAC) meaning: a radical has an unpaired electron. Being a group of atoms is neither necessary (Cl• is one atom) nor sufficient (SO₄²⁻ and NH₄⁺ have all their electrons paired).
items.specStatementText: A radical is a molecular entity that has an unpaired electron. Radicals are highly reactive.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is any highly reactive species a radical?
items.correct: No. Radicals are highly reactive, but many highly reactive species, such as F₂ and Cl₂ molecules, have all their electrons paired and are not radicals.
items.misconception: A radical is identified by high reactivity, so a very reactive substance such as chlorine, Cl₂, or fluorine, F₂, is a radical.
items.why: At GCSE, chlorine and fluorine are the standard examples of "very reactive" elements. In this topic students are then told that radicals are highly reactive, and without practice in counting electrons they classify species by reactivity rather than by structure. High reactivity is a property of radicals, not a test for them. Identify a radical by its structure: count the valence electrons (Cl₂ and F₂ each have 14, all paired) and look for an unpaired one.
items.specStatementText: A radical is a molecular entity that has an unpaired electron. Radicals are highly reactive.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does UV light break a C–H bond of methane in the initiation step?
items.correct: No. The initiation step breaks the Cl–Cl bond (242 kJ mol⁻¹), which is much weaker than the C–H bond (414 kJ mol⁻¹): Cl₂ → 2Cl•. No H• is formed in the chlorination of methane.
items.misconception: In the initiation step the alkane is split: CH₄ → •CH₃ + H•.
items.why: Students see the alkane as the substance 'being reacted', so they expect it to be attacked first, and they write the first step by breaking the bond they will later see replaced (C–H). Initiation breaks the weakest bond available, the halogen–halogen bond. The C–H bond is broken later, in a propagation step, by a Cl• radical: CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl.
items.specStatementText: Radicals are produced by homolytic fission, e.g. of halogens, in the presence of ultraviolet (UV) light or heat.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the low reactivity of alkanes due to strong forces between their molecules?
items.correct: No. The forces between alkane molecules are weak London (dispersion) forces (methane boils at −162 °C). Reactivity depends on the covalent bonds within the molecules.
items.misconception: Alkanes are unreactive because strong intermolecular forces hold their molecules together.
items.why: Students confuse intermolecular forces with covalent bonds within a molecule, a confusion widely documented in chemistry-education research, and use 'strong forces' to explain any kind of stability. Chemical reactions break and form covalent bonds within molecules. Alkanes are stable because those bonds (C–C, C–H) are strong and essentially non-polar, not because of the weak forces between molecules.
items.specStatementText: Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes, producing a mixture of products.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a molecule unreactive because every atom in it has a full outer shell?
items.correct: No. Almost every stable molecule has full outer shells (H₂O, HCl, CH₃Cl), yet many react readily. Reactivity depends on bond strength and polarity, not on whether the shells are full.
items.misconception: Molecules in which every atom has a full outer shell are unreactive, which is why alkanes do not react.
items.why: The 'octet framework' uses full shells to explain every kind of stability; chemistry-education research has documented students carrying it from explaining bonding into explaining reactivity. Full shells explain why a molecule's formula is what it is, not how reactive it is. Compare CH₄ with CH₃Cl: both have full shells, but the polar C–Cl bond makes the chloroalkane far more reactive.
items.specStatementText: Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes, producing a mixture of products.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the C–H bonds in alkanes significantly polar?
items.correct: No. Carbon (2.6) and hydrogen (2.2) have similar electronegativities, so C–H bonds are essentially non-polar and methane does not ionize.
items.misconception: Any bond between two different elements is significantly polar, so the C–H bond in methane can break into ions like the O–H bond in an acid.
items.why: Students are taught that bonds between different atoms are polar and apply the rule without checking the size of the electronegativity difference. Polarity depends on the electronegativity difference. For C–H it is small (0.4), so alkanes are essentially non-polar; this is one reason they are unreactive and why they react with halogens by a radical, not an ionic, mechanism.
items.specStatementText: Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes, producing a mixture of products.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
